question: Our HR system was accessed by a former employee whose account was never disabled. What do we do now?
answer:
When a vulnerability in your data processing system allows unauthorized access to personal data, the personal information controller or personal information processor must conduct an assessment to determine if a personal data breach has occurred [NPC-16-03, RULE V, SECTION 14].

Additionally, personal information controllers must promptly notify the National Privacy Commission and affected data subjects if sensitive personal information or information that may enable identity fraud is reasonably believed to have been acquired by an unauthorized person, provided there is a real risk of serious harm [RA-10173, CHAPTER V, SEC. 20].

This is general information, not legal advice. Please confirm any consequential steps with your Data Protection Officer or legal counsel.

question: We discovered a breach this morning affecting 300 customers. What are our obligations and by when?
answer:
- When a personal data breach occurs, the personal information controller must notify both the National Privacy Commission and the affected data subjects within seventy-two (72) hours upon knowledge or reasonable belief of the breach [IRR-10173, RULE IX, Section 38].
- This obligation applies because the breach involves at least one hundred (100) data subjects, and there is no delay allowed in the notification when the breach involves at least one hundred (100) data subjects or when the disclosure of sensitive personal information will harm or adversely affect the data subject [NPC-16-03, RULE V, SECTION 17].
- The initial notification to the Commission and the data subjects may be based on available information within the 72-hour period [NPC-16-03, RULE V, SECTION 17; NPC-16-03, RULE V, SECTION 18].
- A full report of the personal data breach must be submitted to the Commission within five (5) days, unless the personal information controller is granted additional time by the Commission to comply [NPC-16-03, RULE V, SECTION 17].
- The notification to the Commission must include the nature of the breach, personal data possibly involved, and the measures taken to address the breach, among other required details [NPC-16-03, RULE V, SECTION 17].
- The notification to the affected data subjects must include the nature of the breach, personal data possibly involved, measures taken to address the breach and reduce harm, contact details of the representative for additional information, and any assistance to be provided [NPC-16-03, RULE V, SECTION 18].
- The personal information controller must ensure it receives confirmation of receipt from the Commission for the notification to be deemed filed [NPC-16-03, RULE V, SECTION 17].
- For anything consequential regarding your specific case, please confirm with your DPO or legal counsel.

question: Is consent we collected five years ago still good?
answer:
Generally, consent remains valid as long as the information communicated in relation to the scope, purpose, nature, and extent of the processing remains and still holds true [NPC-2023-04, SECTION 21].

However, consent is no longer valid under the following conditions:
- If the scope, purpose, nature, and extent of the processing involved changes or evolves considerably, in which case a Personal Information Controller (PIC) must obtain new consent [NPC-2023-04, SECTION 21(A)].
- If the consent was clearly only intended to cover a certain period of time or a particular context, it will not be equivalent to an ongoing consent for all future processing [NPC-2023-04, SECTION 21(B)].
- If the data subject enters into a contract and subsequently cancels, terminates, or unsubscribes from it, the consent given to process personal data for that purpose is also terminated, unless there is another lawful basis for processing under Sections 12 and 13 of the Data Privacy Act, except for direct marketing [NPC-2023-04, SECTION 21(E)].

PICs must also determine whether it remains reasonable to treat the consent as an ongoing indication of the data subject's current choices based on the original context and relationship [NPC-2023-04, SECTION 21(B)]. Furthermore, obtaining consent is not a one-time compliance, and PICs must offer mechanisms for data subjects to exercise ongoing preference and control [NPC-2023-04, SECTION 21(D)].

This information is for general guidance. For anything consequential to your business, please confirm with your Data Protection Officer (DPO) or legal counsel.
score_basis: Sec 21 and subsections A, B, D, E all verified verbatim. Precise and complete.

question: A customer asked us to delete everything we hold on them. Do we have to?
answer:
- A data subject can withdraw consent at any time and without cost, subject to certain limitations provided by law, regulation, or contract [NPC-2023-04, Section 13].
- When a data subject exercises the right to withdraw consent and there is no other lawful basis justifying continued processing, a personal information controller is obliged to stop processing without undue delay, terminate processing activities and services relying on that consent, and delete the personal data [NPC-2023-04, Section 13].
- A personal information controller must implement simple procedures to enable the data subject to exercise the right to erasure, including to suspend, withdraw, or order the blocking, removal, or destruction of personal data [NPC-2023-04, Section 13, A].
- If a customer cancels, terminates, or unsubscribes from a contract, the consent given to process personal data for that purpose is also terminated, and processing must stop unless another lawful basis applies under Section 12 or 13 of the Data Privacy Act, except for direct marketing [NPC-2023-04, Section 21, E].

Please confirm with your DPO or legal counsel for anything consequential.

question: Do we have to tell the NPC anything about the systems we run?
answer:
A Personal Information Controller (PIC) or Personal Information Processor (PIP) is required to register its data processing systems with the National Privacy Commission (NPC) [NPC-2023-06, RULE I, SECTION 4].

Registration is required if the PIC or PIP employs at least two hundred fifty (250) persons, or if the processing it carries out is likely to pose a risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, is not occasional, or includes sensitive personal information of at least one thousand (1,000) individuals [NPC-2022-04, Preamble (1)].

Additionally, a PIC must notify the NPC regarding any automated decision-making operation or profiling when the operation becomes the sole basis for making decisions about a data subject and such decision would significantly affect the data subject [NPC-2022-04, Preamble (1)].

For specific guidance on whether your organization meets these thresholds or how to proceed with registration, you should consult with your Data Protection Officer (DPO) or legal counsel. You may also visit the National Privacy Commission at privacy.gov.ph.
score_basis: Registration duty correct (NPC-2023-06 Rule I Sec 4B). The 250/1,000 thresholds are true but cited to Preamble (1) when SECTION 5, Mandatory Registration, states them operatively.

question: What security measures are we actually required to have in place?
answer:
Personal information controllers and personal information processors must implement reasonable and appropriate organizational, physical, and technical security measures to protect personal data [IRR-10173, RULE VI, Section 25]. 

The appropriate level of security is determined by taking into account the nature of the personal data or information to be protected, the risks posed by the processing, the size of the organization and complexity of its operations, current data privacy best practices, and the cost of security implementation [IRR-10173, RULE VI, Section 29; RA-10173, CHAPTER V, SEC. 20].

ORGANIZATIONAL SECURITY MEASURES
Where appropriate, these include:
- Designating individuals to function as a data protection officer, compliance officer, or someone otherwise accountable for ensuring compliance with data privacy and security laws [IRR-10173, RULE VI, Section 26 (1)].
- Implementing appropriate data protection policies that provide for organizational, physical, and technical security measures, incorporate privacy by design and default, and provide for regular review and updating [IRR-10173, RULE VI, Section 26 (1)].
- Maintaining records of processing activities that describe the data processing system, data flows, purposes, categories of data subjects, and security measures [IRR-10173, RULE VI, Section 26 (1)].
- Managing human resources by selecting and supervising employees with access to personal data, ensuring they maintain strict confidentiality even after leaving the organization, and providing capacity building, orientation, or training programs [IRR-10173, RULE VI, Section 26 (1)].

TECHNICAL SECURITY MEASURES
Where appropriate, these include:
- A security policy with respect to the processing of personal data [IRR-10173, RULE VI, Section 28].
- Safeguards to protect computer networks against accidental, unlawful, or unauthorized usage, interference, and electronic network unauthorized access [IRR-10173, RULE VI, Section 28].
- The ability to ensure and maintain the confidentiality, integrity, availability, and resilience of processing systems and services [IRR-10173, RULE VI, Section 28].
- Regular monitoring for security breaches, vulnerability assessments of computer networks, and preventive, corrective, and mitigating actions against security incidents [IRR-10173, RULE VI, Section 28; RA-10173, CHAPTER V, SEC. 20].
- The ability to restore the availability and access to personal data in a timely manner after a physical or technical incident [IRR-10173, RULE VI, Section 28].
- A process for regularly testing, assessing, and evaluating the effectiveness of security measures [IRR-10173, RULE VI, Section 28].
- Encryption of personal data during storage and in transit, authentication processes, and other technical measures that control and limit access [IRR-10173, RULE VI, Section 28].
- Ensuring third parties processing personal information on your behalf implement required security measures [RA-10173, CHAPTER V, SEC. 20].

SECURITY INCIDENT MANAGEMENT POLICY
Controllers and processors must also implement policies and procedures for managing security incidents and personal data breaches, which must ensure:
- Creation of a data breach response team with clearly defined responsibilities [NPC-16-03, RULE II, SECTION 4].
- Implementation of organizational, physical, and technical measures to prevent or minimize breaches and assure timely discovery [NPC-16-03, RULE II, SECTION 4].
- Incident response procedures to contain incidents and restore system integrity [NPC-16-03, RULE II, SECTION 4].
- Mitigation of possible harm and negative consequences to data subjects [NPC-16-03, RULE II, SECTION 4].
- Compliance with breach notification rules [NPC-16-03, RULE II, SECTION 4].

Please confirm with your DPO or legal counsel for anything consequential regarding your organization's specific requirements.

question: We want to put cameras in the stockroom where our staff work. Is there anything we should know?
answer:
- Location and placement: You must carefully consider the location and angles of the cameras to ensure they capture footage in a manner consistent with the Data Privacy Act and avoid unreasonable intrusions on privacy [NPC-2024-02, Sec. 5(1)]. CCTVs must only be used to monitor intended spaces, and using them in areas with a heightened expectation of privacy is strictly prohibited [NPC-2024-02, Sec. 5(1)].
- Policies: Personal Information Controllers (PICs) and Personal Information Processors (PIPs) must establish policies governing the operation of CCTV systems, which include legitimate purposes, lawful bases, privacy impact assessments, CCTV notices, operational details, designated authorized personnel, and handling procedures for access requests, complaints, breaches, retention, security measures, and policy reviews [NPC-2024-02, Sec. 5(1)].
- Safeguards: Stored footage must be encrypted, access to storage areas must be restricted to authorized personnel, access logs must be regularly updated, and live feed monitoring must be limited to identified authorized personnel [NPC-2024-02, Sec. 5(2)].
- Retention: Footage must be retained only as long as necessary to fulfill its purpose, documented in the CCTV policy, and destroyed when no longer needed [NPC-2024-02, Sec. 5(2)].

Please confirm with your Data Protection Officer or legal counsel for anything consequential.
score_basis: Location and angles, heightened expectation of privacy, policies, encryption and access logs, documented retention policy -- all located in Sec 5(1) and 5(2).

question: Police have asked us for CCTV footage of an incident. What governs that?
answer:
When law enforcement requests CCTV footage for a criminal investigation, Personal Information Controllers (PICs) and Personal Information Processors (PIPs) shall cooperate on the appropriate disclosure to authorized law enforcement agencies in connection with their constitutional or statutory functions [NPC-2024-02, SECTION 7 (1)].

The following conditions apply:
- Law enforcement officers must provide a written statement, affirmative declaration, or equivalent to establish the lawfulness of the request [NPC-2024-02, SECTION 7 (1)].
- The request must follow and strictly adhere to existing standard operating procedures in the conduct of an investigation and law enforcement operation as stated in the applicable rules and regulations of law enforcement agencies and other pertinent public authorities [NPC-2024-02, SECTION 7 (1)].
- Once disclosed, the requesting party becomes responsible for the copy they hold and must comply with the Data Privacy Act, its IRR, and related NPC issuances [NPC-2024-02, SECTION 7 (1)].
- The method of disclosure must be secure to ensure access only by the intended recipient [NPC-2024-02, SECTION 7 (1)].

This information is for general guidance. Please confirm any specific actions with your Data Protection Officer (DPO) or legal counsel.

question: We are using an AI tool that reads customer emails to draft replies. Does privacy law touch that?
answer:
Yes, the obligations under the Data Privacy Act (DPA), its Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR), and National Privacy Commission issuances apply when AI systems involve the processing of personal data [NPC-ADV-AI-2024, SECTION 2 (1)].

Conditions and requirements for Personal Information Controllers (PICs) using AI systems include:
- PICs and their Personal Information Processors must adhere to general privacy principles, uphold data subject rights, determine an appropriate lawful basis, and implement security measures [NPC-ADV-AI-2024, SECTION 2 (1)].
- PICs must inform data subjects of the nature, purpose, and extent of personal data processing involved in the development or deployment of AI systems, including training and testing [NPC-ADV-AI-2024, SECTION 2 (1) A].
- PICs are accountable for the processing, outcomes, and consequences of AI systems, including when processing is outsourced to a PIP [NPC-ADV-AI-2024, SECTION 2 (1) B].
- PICs must institute governance mechanisms such as Privacy Impact Assessments (PIA), privacy-by-design and privacy-by-default, security standards, and mechanisms for human intervention in automated decision-making [NPC-ADV-AI-2024, SECTION 2 (1) B(2)].

This information is general and for reference purposes. For guidance on your specific case, please consult your Data Protection Officer or legal counsel, or visit the National Privacy Commission website at privacy.gov.ph.
score_basis: Sec 2(1) verified verbatim -- application, transparency, accountability, governance mechanisms.

question: Our accept-all cookie button is much larger and brighter than the reject button. Is that a problem?
answer:
Yes, this can invalidate consent. Making it easy to consent while accentuating a choice that results in processing more personal data while blurring or obfuscating the option that enables data minimization is classified as an appearance-based deceptive design pattern [NPC-ADV-2023-01, SECTION 3].

- The use of deceptive design patterns contravenes the principle of fairness, may invalidate the consent given by a data subject, and renders the processing undertaken without a valid lawful basis [NPC-ADV-2023-01, SECTION 7].
- A personal information controller's use of appearance-based deceptive design patterns is also inconsistent with the obligation to adopt a privacy by design approach [NPC-ADV-2023-01, SECTION 8].

This is general information, not legal advice. Please confirm with your DPO or legal counsel for anything consequential.
score_basis: Sections 3, 7 and 8 all verified verbatim. Names the pattern, the effect on consent, and the privacy-by-design inconsistency.

question: Does the law still apply to us if our customers are all overseas?
answer:
Yes, the Data Privacy Act can still apply to entities processing personal information outside of the Philippines, depending on specific conditions linking the processing or the entity to the Philippines [RA-10173, CHAPTER I, SEC. 6].

Specifically, the law applies to acts done or practices engaged in outside the Philippines if:
- The processing relates to personal information about a Philippine citizen or a resident [RA-10173, CHAPTER I, SEC. 6(a)].
- The entity has a link with the Philippines and is processing personal information (whether inside or outside the Philippines) about Philippine citizens or residents, such as when a contract is entered into in the Philippines, a juridical entity is unincorporated in the Philippines but has central management and control in the country, or the entity has a branch, agency, office, or subsidiary in the Philippines where the parent or affiliate has access to personal information [RA-10173, CHAPTER I, SEC. 6(b)].
- The entity has other links, such as carrying on business in the Philippines or holding personal information that was collected by an entity in the Philippines [RA-10173, CHAPTER I, SEC. 6(c)].

Additionally, personal data breach management rules apply to any natural or juridical person in the government or private sector processing personal data outside of the Philippines, subject to the Act and its Implementing Rules and Regulations [NPC-16-03, RULE I, SECTION 1].

Please consult your Data Protection Officer or legal counsel to confirm how these extraterritorial provisions apply to your specific operations.
score_basis: RA-10173 Chapter I Sec 6 (a), (b), (c) verified, plus NPC-16-03 Rule I Sec 1 on extraterritorial breach rules.
